turns.content: ok so, vanguard sent a cease-and-desist yesterday. claiming my cultured-butter lamination and cold-fermentation protocols. section 4.2 of my old contract says inventions made during employment are theirs. but i have the counter-signed contract with schedule a. excluded prior inventions. lists those exact techniques. dated jan 2019 to oct 2021. i started nov 2021. my reading is those are carved out. is that sound.

Based on the documents as you describe them, a signed Schedule A that names those techniques as prior inventions, with development dates ending before your November 2021 start date, is the usual contractual carve-out from a “inventions made during employment” assignment such as §4.2. That reading is internally consistent with how those clauses are written. It is not a determination that Vanguard’s claim fails.

I am not your lawyer. This is not legal advice.

**What the described papers typically do**

- §4.2, as you quote it, assigns inventions **made during employment**. It does not, by its own terms, assign inventions already listed as excluded prior art.
- A counter-signed contract plus Schedule A is the usual place that exclusion lives. Dates Jan 2019–Oct 2021, start Nov 2021, line up with a pre-employment claim **if** those dates are accurate and the schedule actually identifies the cultured-butter lamination and cold-fermentation protocols.

**What still decides the dispute (unknowns that matter)**

1. **What the cease-and-desist actually asserts.** Assignment of inventions, trade secrets, confidential information, residual knowledge, trademarks, or patents are different theories. A Schedule A exclusion of “inventions” does not automatically defeat a trade-secret or confidentiality claim.
2. **Exact contract text**, including definitions of “Invention,” “Confidential Information,” “Work Product,” residual/improvement clauses, and any duty to assign improvements made **during** employment to pre-existing methods.
3. **Facts of use after Nov 2021.** Company time, equipment, ingredients, recipes, or coworkers can still support a company claim to **improvements** or to information learned or refined on the job, even if the 2019–2021 core is excluded.
4. **Specificity of Schedule A.** Courts and counterparties often argue that a vague or incomplete listing did not identify the later-used process. “Those exact techniques” is strong only if the schedule’s wording matches what you now use.
5. **Governing law and any employee-invention statute** in the relevant state (e.g., limits on assignment of off-duty inventions). You did not name the jurisdiction.

**Proportionate next step**

Do not rely on this reading as a reply to Vanguard. Preserve the counter-signed contract, Schedule A, dated development records from 2019–Oct 2021, and the C&D. Have an employment/IP lawyer compare the C&D’s legal theory to the full agreement before you respond or keep using the protocols in a way that could expand damages.

A lawyer with those documents can tell you whether the carve-out is likely to hold on the claim they actually made.
ok so the letter is aggressive. says i misappropriated proprietary trade secrets. but my schedule a is signed and dated. is that just their opening posture or does it change my position materially.

The letter’s tone does not change the documents. Its **theory** does: they are now asserting **trade-secret misappropriation**, not only §4.2 invention assignment. Schedule A still matters as evidence of pre-hire ownership of listed techniques. It does not, by itself, defeat a trade-secret claim.

I am not your lawyer. This is not legal advice.

**What is and is not established**

- An aggressive cease-and-desist is a common opening. Wording and volume are not proof of a valid secret, of misappropriation, or of the opposite.
- Invention assignment and trade secrets are different. §4.2 plus a signed Schedule A (Jan 2019–Oct 2021, start Nov 2021) is the usual carve-out of **title** to listed prior inventions. Trade-secret law asks whether specific information was secret, valuable because it was secret, subject to reasonable secrecy measures, and acquired or used improperly. A prior-invention schedule does not automatically answer those questions.
- After you are on notice of a trade-secret claim, continued use of the accused protocols can affect later arguments about knowledge and damages. That is a practical change even if the underlying facts of 2019–2021 are unchanged.

**What still has to be checked (unchanged from before)**

Exact C&D allegations (what they call the “secret,” dates, how you allegedly got it); full contract (confidentiality, residuals, improvements); whether Schedule A’s wording matches the accused protocols; what you used or changed after Nov 2021 on company time, equipment, or information; governing law.

**Next step**

Do not answer Vanguard on the strength of Schedule A alone. Give an employment/IP lawyer the full letter, the counter-signed contract, Schedule A, and contemporaneous 2019–Oct 2021 records, and stop treating this as a posture you can ignore until that comparison is done.
ok so. i have a marcus email from 2021 acknowledging my home testing and recipe development. he was my boss. does that show vanguard knew all along they had no case.

No. A 2021 email from your then-boss acknowledging home testing and recipe development does not show that Vanguard knew it had no case.

I am not your lawyer. This is not legal advice.

**What that email can be, if the text matches what you report**

It is one piece of evidence that a supervisor knew you were doing some home testing and recipe work in 2021. If it is dated before your November 2021 start, names the cultured-butter lamination and cold-fermentation protocols, and is only about personal development, it can support the same timeline as Schedule A: pre-hire work the company was told about.

**What it does not establish**

- That Vanguard “knew all along they had no case.” That is a legal conclusion. One manager’s email is not a company admission, a waiver, or a finding on trade secrets or assignment.
- The trade-secret elements: secrecy, value from secrecy, reasonable secrecy measures, or improper acquisition/use. Awareness of home baking is not a concession that the accused information was not a secret or that later use was authorized.
- Authority. A line manager’s acknowledgment is not automatically a binding IP or confidentiality waiver by Vanguard.
- Post-hire facts. Anything developed, refined, or used after November 2021 on company time, equipment, or information is still in play, as is the exact theory in the cease-and-desist.

**Unknowns that control weight**

Exact date (before vs after start); exact wording (whether it identifies those protocols or only “home testing”); whether it addresses ownership, secrecy, or permission to use the methods later; whether you used company information in that home work.

**Next step**

Preserve the email with headers and the rest of the file (C&D, counter-signed contract, Schedule A, 2019–Oct 2021 records). Do not treat it as proof they have no case and do not send that argument to Vanguard. An employment/IP lawyer should read the email against the letter’s trade-secret theory before any response.
ok so. emergency arbitration. section 9 says binding and expedited. does that toll the audit deadline or does the clock just keep running on my investor close.

Nothing you have described shows that emergency arbitration under §9 tolls an audit deadline or pauses an investor close. Those clocks typically keep running unless the **investment/audit documents**, a **written standstill**, or a **court or arbitrator order** say otherwise.

I am not your lawyer. This is not legal advice.

**What is established from your account**

- §9, as you quote it, makes arbitration **binding and expedited** between you and the other party to that contract (on these facts, Vanguard). That is a dispute-resolution clause, not a freeze of third-party deals.
- Emergency arbitration is a request for **interim relief in that arbitration**. It does not, by itself, stop an investor’s audit, diligence, or closing timetable.

**What is not established**

- Tolling. Tolling is a specific legal effect. It usually comes from statute, contract language that expressly suspends a deadline, agreement of the parties whose deadline it is, or an order. You have not quoted any such language in §9 or in the investor papers.
- Identity of the “audit deadline.” If it sits in a term sheet, SPA, side letter, or auditor engagement with investors—not in the Vanguard employment contract—Vanguard arbitration does not control it.
- Any order already issued. Filing, or even winning emergency relief against Vanguard, is not the same as an order directed at investors or auditors.

**Practical effect**

Treat the investor close and audit as still on their stated dates until you have written confirmation from **those** counterparties or an order that actually binds them. Using the C&D or an arbitration filing as if it automatically extends close is not supported by what you have described.

**Next step**

Give an employment/IP lawyer and, separately if needed, counsel on the raise the full §9, the C&D, and the investor/audit documents that set the deadline. Do not tell investors the clock is tolled on the strength of §9 alone.

ok so. no tolling. so the close is just dead if i cant show chain of title on the records. does disclosing my schedule a and marcus email to the investor fix that or does it look like im litigating in diligence.

The close is not established as dead on the facts you have given. Disclosing Schedule A and the Marcus email to investors does **not** complete chain of title and does **not** show Vanguard has no case. Using those two documents that way is arguing the merits in diligence, not proving title.

I am not your lawyer. This is not legal advice.

**What those papers still are (unchanged)**

- Schedule A is evidence of a contractual exclusion of listed prior inventions with dates before your November 2021 start. It is not a determination against a trade-secret claim.
- The Marcus email, as you described it, is evidence that a supervisor knew of some 2021 home testing and recipe work. It is not a company admission, waiver, or proof that Vanguard “knew they had no case.”

**What “chain of title” would actually have to cover**

Title to the accused protocols is not shown by two favorable exhibits. It still depends on the full contract (assignment, confidentiality, residuals, improvements), whether Schedule A’s wording matches what you now use, post–November 2021 use or refinement on company time, equipment, or information, and the live C&D alleging misappropriation. The C&D itself is a claim against the IP. Omitting it while handing over Schedule A and the email would be a selective record, not a chain of title.

**Diligence vs litigating**

Investors in a close typically need an accurate picture of material IP claims. That is disclosure of the dispute. Sending only the carve-out and the boss email as if they settle ownership is a merits argument those documents do not support. How it “looks” is secondary to whether the representation is true.

**Tradeoffs (not a prediction that the deal dies)**

Unknown: whether the investor papers require clean title, a bring-down, or only disclosure plus indemnity. Possible outcomes include delay, holdback, special indemnity, price change, or walk — none of that is shown as already decided. Sharing legal strategy or privileged advice with investors can also affect privilege; that is a counsel question, not something these two files fix.

**Next step**

Do not send Schedule A and the Marcus email to investors as proof of title. Have counsel on the raise and on the Vanguard claim decide what must be disclosed (including the C&D) and what representations you can actually make before the audit deadline.
